'''''Lilium martagon''''', the '''martagon lily'''<ref name=BSBI07>{{BSBI 2007 |access-date=2014-10-17 }}</ref> or '''Turk's cap lily''', is a Eurasian species of [[Lilium|lily]]. It has a widespread [[native plant|native]] region extending from [[Portugal]] east through Europe and [[Asia]] as far east as [[Mongolia]].<ref name=gerta>{{cite web|url=http://apps.kew.org/wcsp/namedetail.do?name_id=279985|title=World Checklist of Selected Plant Families: Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew}}</ref><ref>[http://luirig.altervista.org/flora/taxa/index1.php?scientific-name=lilium+martagon Altervista Flora Italiana, Giglio a turbante, Common Turk's Cap Lily, ''Lilium martagon'' L.] includes many color photos plus European distribution map</ref><ref>[http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=2&taxon_id=240001420 Flora of China, Vol. 24 Page 137 <big>新疆百合</big> xin jiang bai he ''Lilium martagon'' var. ''pilosiusculum'' Freyn, Oesterr. Bot. Z. 40: 224. 1890.]</ref><ref>Tutin, T.G. & al. (eds.) (1980). Flora Europaea 5: 1-452. Cambridge University Press.</ref><ref>Davis, P.H. (ed.) (1984). Flora of Turkey and the East Aegean Islands 8: 1-632. Edinburgh University Press, Edinburgh.</ref><ref>Czerepanov, S.K. (1995). Vascular Plants of Russia and Adjacent States (The Former USSR): 1-516. Cambridge University Press.</ref><ref>Grubov, V.I. (2001). Key to the Vascular Plants of Mongolia 1: 1-411. Science Publishers, Inc. Enfield, USA. Plymouth, U.K.</ref><ref>Ikinci, N., Oberprieler, C. & Güner, A. (2006). On the origin of European lilies: phylogenetic analysis of ''Lilium'' section ''Liriotypus'' (Liliaceae) using sequences of the nuclear ribosomal transcribed spacers. Willdenowia 36: 647-565.</ref>

==Description==
It is stem-rooting, growing between {{convert|1|m}} and {{convert|2|m}} tall. The flower colour is typically a pink-purple, with dark spots, but is quite variable, extending from near white to near black. The flowers are scented. Numerous flowers are borne on each plant, and up to 50 can be found on vigorous plants. The green stems can be flushed with purple or red and the leaves are elliptic to inverse [[lanceolate]], mostly in whorls, up to {{convert|16|cm}} long and often lightly hairy underneath.<ref>{{cite book|author=Christopher Brickell|title=The RHS Encyclopedia of Garden Plants|publisher=[[Dorling Kindersley]]|place=[[London]]|year=1996|page=615|isbn=0-7513-0436-0}}</ref><ref>European Garden Flora, 1986.</ref>

==Varieties==
Numerous names have been proposed at the levels of subspecies and varieties. Only two are recognized by the [[World Checklist of Selected Plant Families|World Checklist]].<ref name=gerta/>
*''Lilium martagon'' var. ''martagon'' – from [[Portugal]] to [[Mongolia]]
*''Lilium martagon'' var. ''pilosiusculum'' <small>Freyn</small> – [[Russia]], [[Kazakhstan]], [[Xinjiang]], [[Mongolia]]

==Cultivation==
Horticulturally it is in [[Lilium#Classification of garden forms|Division IX]] (true species). 

This plant<ref>{{cite web|title=RHS Plant Selector - ''Lilium martagon''|url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/10205/Lilium-martagon-(IXc-d)/Details | access-date = 16 January 2021}}</ref> has gained the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]].<ref>{{cite web | url= https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/pdfs/agm-lists/agm-ornamentals.pdf | title = AGM Plants - Ornamental | date = July 2017 | page = 20 | publisher = Royal Horticultural Society | access-date = 22 March 2018}}</ref> 

''Lilium martagon'' was used in hybridising with ''[[Lilium hansonii|L. hansonii]]'' at the end of the 19th century by Mrs RO Backhouse of Hereford, England.<ref>Andrew Mikolajski, The New Plant Library - Lilies, Lorenz Books, Anness Publishing Ltd, New York, 1998, p10, {{ISBN|1-85967-634-0}}</ref>

==Name==
The name '''Turk's cap lily''', also applied to a number of other species, comes from the characteristic reflexed shape of the petals.<ref>{{cite book|author=Allen J Coombes|title=The Hamlyn Guide to Plant Names|publisher=[[Reed Elsevier|Reed International Books]]|year=1985|page=118|isbn=0-600-57545-4}}</ref> The [[Binomial nomenclature|specific epithet]] ''martagon'' is of uncertain origin.<ref name=RHSLG>{{cite book | last=Harrison |first=Lorraine | title=RHS Latin for Gardeners | year=2012 |publisher=Mitchell Beazley | location=United Kingdom | isbn=978-1845337315 }}</ref> It has been suggested by one scholar (J.W. Redhouse (1892), that the word is of Ottoman Turkish origin, as ''mārtağān'' - a special kind of turban adopted by Sultan Muhammed.<ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.oed.com/view/Entry/114411?redirectedFrom=martagon#eid | url-access = subscription | title = martagon | website = Oxford English Dictionary online | publisher = OED | access-date = 8 November 2021}}</ref> However, the word is not found in modern Turkish.

==Toxicity==

===Cats===
''Lilium martagon'', like many in the genus, is highly toxic to [[cats]] and ingestion often leads to fatal [[kidney failure]];<ref>[http://www.noliliesforcats.com/faq1.pml Frequently Asked Questions] No Lilies For Cats.</ref><ref>{{cite journal | pmid = 21147474 | doi=10.1053/j.tcam.2010.09.006 | volume=25 | title=Lily toxicity in the cat | year=2010 | journal=Top Companion Anim Med | pages=213–7 | last1 = Fitzgerald | first1 = KT| issue=4 }}</ref><ref>[https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle/2013/jul/21/turks-cap-lily-is-pure-delight Turk's cap lily is pure delight] The Guardian.</ref> households and gardens which are visited by cats are strongly advised against keeping this plant or placing dried flowers where a cat may brush against them and become dusted with pollen which they then consume while cleaning. Suspected cases require urgent veterinary attention.<ref name="petmd" /> Rapid treatment with [[activated charcoal]] and/or induced [[vomiting]] can reduce the amount of toxin absorbed (this is time-sensitive so in some cases vets may advise doing it at home), and large amounts of fluid by [[Intravenous injection|IV]] can reduce damage to kidneys to increase the chances of survival.<ref name="petmd">[http://www.petmd.com/cat/emergency/poisoning-toxicity/e_ct_lily_poisoning Lily Poisoning in Cats]. Pet MD.</ref>
